b.v: Today's goal

v: Understand why light matters more than the camera
Shoot your first photo in natural daylight
See the difference between hard and soft light

b.v: About 20 minutes. Do this in the morning or late afternoon.
Good product photos are mostly good light. A simple phone in soft daylight beats an expensive camera under a tube light. So do not shop for gear today. Learn to see where the light is coming from.
1) Find the free light in your home
A window is a large soft light source, and it is free. It is the single best studio most people already own.

v: A window that does not get direct harsh sun is best
Morning and late afternoon give the softest light
Side light shows texture and shape
Front light flattens but is safe and easy

b.v: 2) Hard light versus soft light
Hard light makes sharp dark shadows. Soft light makes gentle shadows and shows the whole product. Product photos usually want soft.

Compare them:|Place a product near a window and photograph it|Move it into direct noon sun and photograph again|Compare the shadows in both images|Then hold a sheet of white paper between sun and product and shoot a third time
3) Three directions, three looks
Where the light sits changes what the buyer believes about the material.

v: Side light: shows fabric folds and surface texture
Front light: safe, flat, good for documents and labels
Back light: rim glow, dramatic, useful for glass and liquids
Top light alone: makes harsh shadows under the product

b.v: Do not use the phone flash. It is a tiny hard light two centimetres from the lens and it makes plastic look cheap, creates hot spots and flattens every texture.
Practice
Photograph one product in three places: near a window, in direct sun, and in a dark corner. Open all three on your phone and write one line on which light you would buy from.

day-2.t: Day 2 — Phone settings that actually matter

b.v: Today's goal

v: Set up the camera app once, properly
Learn focus and exposure lock
Stop the automatic settings that ruin photos

b.v: About 20 minutes. Use your own phone's camera app.
Your phone camera is good enough. The defaults are tuned for faces and landscapes, not for a bedsheet on a table. Four small changes make it behave.
1) Clean the lens and turn off the extras
A smudge on the lens creates a soft glow that looks like a bad camera. It is almost always a fingerprint.

v: Wipe the lens with a soft cloth before every shoot
Turn off the flash
Turn off beauty mode and any face smoothing
Turn off the watermark and date stamp
Use the main camera, not the wide angle, unless you need the extra view

b.v: 2) Focus and exposure lock
Automatic focus hunts while you move, and automatic exposure brightens the whole frame when a white background fills it. Lock both.

Lock them:|Open the camera and point at the product|Tap and hold on the product until a lock indicator appears|Drag the small sun slider up or down to set brightness|Keep the phone still and take the shot|Repeat for each new angle, the lock resets when you move
3) The settings worth changing
These four are in most camera apps. Look for them once and they will help every photo after.

v: Grid lines on, to keep the product straight
Highest resolution and quality available
Save as the standard format, not a live photo
HDR off if it makes whites look grey, on if shadows are too dark

b.v: Do not zoom with your fingers. Digital zoom simply crops and blurs. Move closer with your feet, or crop slightly later.
Practice
Take one photo with automatic settings and one with focus and exposure locked on the product. Compare the whites. The locked version should look more consistent.

day-3.t: Day 3 — Build a studio for almost nothing

b.v: Today's goal

v: Set up a permanent shooting corner
Use household items as a softbox and reflector
Make a tabletop background in five minutes

b.v: About 25 minutes. Everything here can be found at home.
A studio is not a room full of equipment. It is a table near a window with a clean surface and something white to bounce light back. Total cost: close to zero.
1) What you actually need
Five items, and you probably own four of them.

v: A table near a window, at about waist height
A large white sheet or a roll of white chart paper
A whiteboard, foam board or a sheet of paper as a reflector
A phone stand, or a stack of books and a rubber band
A cloth to clean the product and the lens

b.v: 2) Assemble the corner
The goal is a smooth curve from the table to the wall, so there is no visible horizon line behind the product.

Build it:|Clear the table and put it beside the window, light coming from one side|Tape a large white sheet to the wall and let it curve onto the table|Place the product on the curved part, not at the seam|Put the reflector on the shadow side, facing the product|Stand so the window is to your left or right, never behind you
3) Soften harsh light for free
If the shadows are too sharp, you need a bigger light surface, not a better camera.

v: Tape a white plastic bag or thin white cloth over the window
Never let the cloth touch the product, it will show texture
Move the product further from the window to soften more
Use a second white sheet on the shadow side to fill it

b.v: Do not shoot on a bedsheet with visible wrinkles, or on a printed tablecloth. The camera records every wrinkle and the product looks careless.
Practice
Build the corner today and leave it standing for the rest of the course. Shoot one product on it and check the background has no visible seam.

day-4.t: Day 4 — Backgrounds that do not fight the product

b.v: Today's goal

v: Choose between white, coloured and lifestyle backgrounds
Keep the product the brightest thing in the frame
Shoot one product on three different backgrounds

b.v: About 20 minutes. Use paper, cloth and a plain wall.

A background is not decoration. It tells the buyer where the product belongs. A plain white background says catalogue. A wooden table says home. A bright colour says playful. The wrong one makes people scroll past.
1) White is the default for a reason
Marketplaces often require a plain white main image. It also makes the product colour accurate and easy to compare.

v: Use white for the first image in almost every case
A slight grey is safer than pure white, it keeps edges visible
White products need a light grey or a shadow to show shape
Avoid a white product on a pure white background with no shadow

b.v: 2) When colour helps
A colour background helps when the product itself is simple and needs contrast, or when the brand has one clear colour.

Test a colour:|Pick a colour that appears in the product or its packaging|Place the product two hand spans from the background to avoid colour spill|Check that the product edge still separates from the background|Shoot with and without it, then compare at thumbnail size
Do not use a busy background with patterns, other products or a cluttered room. The eye goes to the clutter and the product becomes the background.
3) Lifestyle shots sell the feeling
A lifestyle photo shows the product being used. It answers the question: where would this live in my life?

v: Use a real surface, a table, a shelf, a hand
Keep the setting simple, one or two props at most
Match the light direction to your catalogue shots
Shoot the lifestyle version second, never as the main image

b.v: Practice
Shoot the same product on white, on one colour and in a simple lifestyle setting. View all three as small thumbnails and pick the one that makes the product clearest.

day-5.t: Day 5 — Angles that show what matters

b.v: Today's goal

v: Learn the five angles worth shooting
Match the angle to the product type
Shoot a complete set in one session

b.v: About 25 minutes. Move your feet, not the zoom.
One photo cannot answer every question. A set of five angles answers shape, size, texture, use and contents. That is usually enough to sell without a video.
1) The five angles
Shoot in this order every time. It becomes a habit and your catalogue looks consistent.

v: Front, straight on, camera at product height
Three quarter, slightly above and to one side
Side, to show depth and thickness
Close up, to show material and finish
Top down flat lay, everything in the box laid out

b.v: 2) Camera height decides the mood
Where you hold the phone is a choice. Each height says something different.

Try three heights:|Eye level with the product, honest and neutral|Slightly above, the most flattering for most objects|Straight down from above, best for flat items and sets|Pick the height that matches your category|Keep the same height across the catalogue
Do not shoot everything from standing height looking down. It makes products look small and hides the front of bottles, boxes and shoes.
3) Keep verticals straight
A crooked product looks like a rushed photo. Use the grid and check the edges before you press the button.

v: Turn the grid on in the camera app
Line the product edge with a grid line
Keep the phone level, both hands, elbows close
Step back and crop later if you need more room

b.v: Practice
Shoot all five angles for one product today, keeping the camera at the same height each time. Delete any shot where the product edge is crooked.
Today's goal

v: Stop size confusion with one photo
Use references that make sense in Pakistan
Write measurements in the description too

b.v: About 15 minutes. One hand, one common object, one ruler.
Size is the number one cause of returns, and the fix is one extra photo. A product on a plain background gives no clue whether it is ten centimetres or one metre.
1) Use a familiar reference
The reference must be something the buyer sees daily, so the brain can compare instantly.

v: A hand holding the product, the most useful reference
A mobile phone, everyone knows its size
A standard water bottle or a tea cup
A ruler or measuring tape, for exact sizes

b.v: 2) Shoot the scale photo
Keep it simple and honest. A hand that hides the product is worse than no hand at all.

Shoot it:|Place the product on the same background as the others|Hold or place the reference beside it, not in front|Keep both in focus, so move back a little|Shoot at the same camera height as your front shot|Add one line of text with the exact size in the description
3) Write the measurements
A photo reduces confusion. A number removes it. Use both.

v: Length, width and height in centimetres
Weight in grams or kilograms
For clothing, chest and length, not only S M L
For sets, the size of each piece separately

b.v: Do not photograph a small product next to something huge to make it look bigger. Buyers notice on arrival, and that becomes a return and a bad review.
Practice
Shoot one scale photo with a hand and one with a ruler. Then write the exact measurements in centimetres for that product.

day-7.t: Day 7 — Edit in a free app, in five minutes

b.v: Today's goal

v: Make four edits that fix most photos
Keep colours honest
Save a preset you can reuse

b.v: About 20 minutes. Use whichever free editor you already have.
Editing is correction, not decoration. You are fixing the camera's guesses about brightness and colour. If a buyer receives something that looks different from the photo, the edit cost you a sale.
1) The four edits that matter
Do these in order. Stop when it looks like the product in real life.

Edit in this order:|Crop and straighten, keep the product centred with equal space|Adjust exposure slightly, so whites are white not grey|Adjust white balance, so a white sheet looks white not blue or yellow|Raise shadows a little, so the dark side is not black|Sharpen slightly, do not overdo it
2) Remove the background only when you must
A clean white background is required by many marketplaces. A free background removal tool does this well for simple shapes, badly for hair, glass and thin straps.

v: Check the edges at full size before you save
Add a soft shadow so the product does not float
Never remove the background from a photo of a person's hand
Keep the original file, you may need to redo it

b.v: Do not use heavy beauty filters, strong saturation or a colour tint on a product photo. The colour must match what arrives in the parcel.
3) Save a preset
A preset is a saved set of adjustments. It makes a whole catalogue look like one shop instead of ten different ones.

v: Edit your best photo until it looks right
Save those settings as a preset or copy them
Apply to the next photo, then adjust exposure only
Name the preset by product type, for example clothing or boxes

b.v: Practice
Edit one photo using the four steps, then save the settings as a preset. Apply that preset to a second photo and change only the exposure.

day-8.t: Day 8 — Make the catalogue look like one shop

b.v: Today's goal

v: Set rules for background, size and order
Fix an existing inconsistent set
Write your own one page photo standard

b.v: About 20 minutes. Open your current product photos.
Consistency is what makes a small shop look professional. When every photo has the same background, the same crop and the same order, the shop feels organised and the products are easier to compare.
1) Write the standard down
A standard is five lines that anyone helping you can follow. Without it, every new photo drifts a little.

v: Background: one white sheet, one colour, one surface
Crop: square, product filling about 80 percent of the frame
Light: window on the left, every time
Order: front, three quarter, side, close up, scale, flat lay
Editing: one preset for the whole catalogue

b.v: 2) Fix the set you already have
Do not reshoot everything. Fix the first image of each product, because that is the one buyers see in a list.

Fix in this order:|List your products and open the first image of each|Delete any image with a watermark, text or a messy room|Reshoot only the first images that break the standard|Apply the preset to all of them|View the whole grid on your phone as a buyer would
3) Name and store the files
You will have hundreds of photos soon. A naming rule saves hours of searching.

v: Name: product name, then angle number
Keep originals in one folder and edited copies in another
Compress before upload, under about 150 KB per image
Back the folder up to cloud storage once a month

b.v: Do not upload ten megabyte photos straight from the phone. They make your shop slow on mobile data, and slow pages lose sales before the photo is even seen.
Practice
Write your five line photo standard today and apply the preset to every first image in your catalogue. Then look at the grid on your phone.

day-9.t: Day 9 — Short video clips that work in ads

b.v: Today's goal

v: Shoot a simple product clip with your phone
Understand the first three seconds
Make one clip that can be reused everywhere

b.v: About 25 minutes. Shoot vertically, hold the phone steady.
A short vertical clip does something a photo cannot: it shows how the product moves, folds, opens or pours. You do not need a script or a model. You need one clear action and good light.
1) Plan three seconds first
People decide in the first moments. Start with the product already visible and moving, not with a logo or a blank wall.

v: Start with the product in frame and something happening
One action only: opening, folding, pouring, wearing
Keep it between ten and twenty seconds
End with the product still, so a screenshot works as a photo

b.v: 2) Shoot it steadily
Shaky footage looks amateur immediately. Rest the phone on something.

Shoot the clip:|Set the phone to the video mode and the highest quality you need|Stand it on books or a stand, vertical|Frame the product with the window light on one side|Tap and hold to lock focus and exposure|Start recording, do the action slowly, stop|Record three takes, choose the best
Do not add loud music you do not own the rights to. Platforms mute or remove the video, and paid ads get rejected.
3) Add simple text, then stop
Most people watch with sound off. One line of text explains the clip.

v: One line only, large enough to read on a phone
Say what it is, or the price, or the size
Add the text in the free editor, not in the camera
No flashing effects, no stickers covering the product

b.v: Practice
Record three takes of one ten second product action, pick the steadiest, add one line of text and save it. Watch it once with the sound off.

day-10.t: Day 10 — The fifteen minute repeatable workflow

b.v: Today's goal

v: Follow one fixed routine per product
Photograph a new product in fifteen minutes
Keep a checklist so nothing is missed

b.v: About 25 minutes. Do a full timed run today.
Speed comes from routine, not from rushing. Once the corner is built and the preset is saved, a product takes about fifteen minutes: five to set up, five to shoot, five to edit and upload.
1) The routine
Same steps every time. Do not improvise, that is where the extra hour goes.

Run the fifteen minutes:|Minute 0 to 3, clean the product and the lens, set it on the background|Minute 3 to 5, check the light and lock focus and exposure|Minute 5 to 10, shoot the six standard frames|Minute 10 to 13, apply the preset and fix exposure on each image|Minute 13 to 15, compress, rename and upload
2) The checklist
Write it once and keep it near the table. A checklist removes the small forgotten steps that cause reshoots.

v: Lens clean, product clean
Grid on, flash off, phone steady
Six frames shot, none crooked
Preset applied, colour honest
Files under about 150 KB and named correctly

b.v: Do not skip the check on your phone screen at full size. A photo that looks fine small often shows dust, a hair or a smudge when a buyer zooms in.
3) Measure, then improve one thing
Time the routine for a week, then change one variable. That is how a hobby becomes a system.

v: Time your first full run and write it down
Find the step that took longest
Change one thing about that step next time
Compare your new photos with last month's, side by side

b.v: Practice
Photograph one complete product today using the fifteen minute routine, with a timer. Write the real time it took and the one step you will speed up next.
